lines: Kyle Grieve and Shawn O'Malley argue Canadian Pacific Kansas City, the only single-network railroad linking Canada, the US and Mexico, has an irreplaceable moat, but its compounding since the 2023 Kansas City Southern deal is still unproven.

They say the moat rests on huge capital needs, land rights and regulation that make a competing network virtually impossible, while captive shippers built into a specific line give railroads their strongest pricing power.
Precision-scheduled railroading, which runs trains on fixed airline-like schedules instead of holding for tonnage, is credited with lifting margins through less idle time and better locomotive use.

The hosts note the KCS acquisition added debt, goodwill and share dilution, leaving ROIC below historical highs, and caution that fuel surcharges can inflate headline revenue without adding real growth.

Their verdict: regulators cap pricing to protect captive shippers, rail still loses short, time-sensitive freight to trucks, and the stock trades near intrinsic value, implying steady mid-single-digit compounding rather than big upside.
